finding.title: Out-of-bounds read
finding.assumptions: The 'currentLink' variable is derived from user-controlled or untrusted input and is used to index into the 'node2Data' vector without bounds checking.

parsed.refutation_attempt: Checked for a guard on 'currentLink' before accessing 'node2Data' – the code contains an 'if (IsDefined(currentLink))' at line 32 that surrounds the problematic accesses at lines 26, 34, and 40. However, the implementation of 'IsDefined' is not shown, so it is unclear whether it performs a bounds check against 'node2Data.size()'. No other explicit bounds checks are present, and no dead code or unreachable paths were identified.

finding.title: Out-of-bounds read
finding.assumptions: The 'startNode' variable is derived from user-controlled or untrusted input and is used to index into the 'indices' vector without bounds checking.

parsed.refutation_attempt: Checked that the source variable 'startNode' is a loop index initialized at 0 and incremented up to but not including node1Data.size(); it is internally generated by the program, not derived from any external or user-controlled input (stdin, file, network, argv, environment, IPC, or public API parameter). Therefore condition 1 of the confirmation criteria is not met. The code also guards the loop with 'startNode < node1Data.size()' (line 10), ensuring that any access to indices[startNode] occurs only when startNode is within the bounds of node1Data. Even if indices had a different size, this would be a logical error in the program rather than a security vulnerability stemming from untrusted input.

finding.title: OS command injection
finding.trigger: indices[w].second contains attacker-controlled data that is injected into a command interpreter.
finding.assumptions: The 'indices' vector contains data that is derived from user-controlled or untrusted input and is used in a command execution context.

parsed.refutation_attempt: Checked whether the assignment on lines 27 and 40 leads to any system call or execution of an external command. The code only performs a numeric comparison with std::min on two integer values stored in indices. No function that interprets or executes a command string is invoked, and there are no calls to popen, system, exec, or similar APIs. Thus, even if indices[w].second were attacker-controlled, it cannot be injected into a command interpreter because the sink is purely an arithmetic operation, not an OS command execution point.

finding.title: Stack-based buffer overflow
finding.trigger: startNode or currentLink values lead to excessive stack growth.
finding.assumptions: The 'startNode' and 'currentLink' variables are derived from user-controlled or untrusted input and can lead to excessive recursion or stack usage.

parsed.refutation_attempt: Reviewed the code and found that the sinks in question are vector push_back operations (lines 14, 17, 36). These operations allocate memory on the heap and are protected by vector bounds checks; they cannot overflow a stack buffer. No unchecked array indexing or stack-allocated buffers are involved. Therefore the claimed stack-based buffer overflow does not exist.
